Part 1 of 9

Foreign Policy and National Security

CORE OBJECTIVE

FQ 1: Essential Question: How does the United States strategically balance the pursuit of national interests with the promotion of global democratic values?

IN MY WORDS: What is foreign policy, and why do Americans disagree about it?

Reading APearl Harbor Ends an Era

On December 8, 1941 — the morning after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor — Franklin Roosevelt appeared before a joint session of Congress and asked for a declaration of war against Japan. Congress complied within hours, with only a single dissenting vote. Three days later, Germany and Italy declared war on the United States, and Congress responded with unanimous declarations of war against both countries. Within the span of four days, the United States had entered a global conflict on two fronts, ending more than two decades of determined effort to remain outside the quarrels of the old world.

The attack on Pearl Harbor did not merely launch America into World War II; it ended, conclusively and permanently, the strategic doctrine of isolationism that had guided American foreign policy since George Washington's Farewell Address a century and a half earlier. The transformation was not just strategic but psychological. Americans who had watched European and Asian conflicts escalate through the 1930s while insisting that these wars were not America's problem discovered, on December 7, 1941, that the oceans that had seemed to provide a reliable barrier against foreign entanglement were no protection at all in an era of modern warfare.

The lesson of Pearl Harbor — that American security was inextricably linked to conditions in Europe and Asia, and that threats distant from American shores could rapidly become threats to the American homeland — became the defining premise of American foreign policy for the remainder of the twentieth century and into the twenty-first.

Word help: declaration of war = a formal statement by Congress that the country is at war · dissenting vote = a vote against · isolationism = staying out of other countries' conflicts · entanglement = being pulled into others' problems · foreign policy = the goals and actions a country uses in dealing with other countries · national security = protecting the country and its people from threats · homeland = one's own country

Reading BA Debate Every Generation Has Had

That premise has never been uncontested. Every generation of Americans has debated, sometimes bitterly, how deeply the United States should involve itself in the affairs of the wider world — how much it should spend on defense and foreign assistance, when it should use military force, how much weight it should give to international institutions and alliances, and whether the promotion of democracy and human rights abroad is a genuine strategic interest or an idealistic distraction from the harder work of protecting American economic and security interests in an anarchic international system. These debates reflect genuine disagreements about both the nature of the international environment and the proper role of American power within it

Word help: contested = argued about · anarchic = without a central ruler or police · international system = how the countries of the world relate · realism = the view that power and national interest drive world affairs · idealism = the view that values and institutions can improve world affairs · institutional structures = the offices and rules that turn plans into action · hegemony = leadership by the strongest power

Part 2 of 9

Realism and Idealism

CORE OBJECTIVES

FQ 2: Contrast the competing philosophies of realism and idealism in American foreign policy, explaining how each framework diagnoses the international environment and prescribes different strategies for pursuing American interests and values abroad.

FQ 1: Essential Question: How does the United States strategically balance the pursuit of national interests with the promotion of global democratic values?

IN MY WORDS: How would a realist and an idealist each decide whether to help another country?

Reading CRealism: Power and Interest

Realism, as a theory of international relations, begins from a specific and sobering diagnosis of the international system: it is a condition of anarchy. Unlike domestic societies, which are governed by laws backed by legitimate authority that can compel compliance, the international system has no central government, no police force, and no reliable mechanism for enforcing agreements or punishing aggression. In this anarchic environment, nations can ultimately rely only on their own power to protect their interests, and the primary currency of international politics is not law or morality but power — military capability, economic strength, and the credible willingness to use both.

The implications of this diagnosis for foreign policy are significant. If the international system is anarchic and power is its primary currency, then the primary obligation of foreign policy is to protect the nation's vital interests — above all its security and its economic welfare — rather than to pursue abstract moral objectives. Alliances are valuable when they enhance national power; they should be dissolved or renegotiated when they no longer serve this purpose. International institutions are useful when they constrain the behavior of rivals more than they constrain the behavior of the United States; they should be treated with skepticism when they impose obligations that limit American freedom of action without corresponding benefits. The promotion of democracy, human rights, and other idealistic objectives has its place, but it must always be subordinated to the harder calculus of national interest when the two conflict.

Word help: anarchy = no central government over countries · currency = here, the main form of value · vital interests = needs a country cannot give up · credible = believable · subordinated = placed second · skepticism = doubt · obligations = duties

Chapter 18, Section I, “Realism: The Logic of Power and Interest.”

Reading DThe Balance of Power

Realist thinking has informed some of the most consequential American foreign policy decisions of the twentieth century. Richard Nixon's opening to China in 1972 — the decision to establish diplomatic relations with the communist People's Republic of China, which the United States had refused to recognize for more than two decades — was a classic exercise in realist statecraft, driven not by any sympathy with Chinese communism but by the calculation that a relationship with China would strengthen the American strategic position relative to the Soviet Union, forcing the USSR to contend with a potential adversary on its eastern flank while managing the American challenge on its western one.

Henry Kissinger, Nixon's national security advisor and the architect of the China opening, was perhaps the most systematic practitioner of realist foreign policy in American history, consistently prioritizing the balance of power over ideological considerations in a manner that produced strategic successes alongside serious moral controversies. The concept of the "balance of power" is central to realist strategic thinking. Realists argue that international stability is best maintained not when any single nation is overwhelmingly dominant — since dominance invites challenges from coalitions of states that fear domination — but when power is roughly distributed among several major actors who check each other's ambitions.

American foreign policy has at various points been guided by this principle: the commitment to preventing any single power from dominating Europe or Asia, which drew the United States into both world wars and sustained its Cold War alliances, reflects a realist understanding that American security depends on maintaining a balance of power in the world's most strategically significant regions.

Word help: statecraft = skill in running a country's relations · People's Republic of China = the communist government of mainland China · USSR = the Soviet Union · adversary = an enemy or rival · balance of power = a situation where no one country is far stronger than the rest · dominant = in control

Chapter 18, Section I, “Realism: The Logic of Power and Interest.”

Realism in action. Reading D says Nixon's opening to China was "a classic exercise in realist statecraft." What was his reason, and why is it realist rather than idealist?

Reading EIdealism: Values and Democratic Peace

Idealism — sometimes called liberal internationalism in its contemporary form — begins from a fundamentally different premise about the international system and about what produces stability and peace. Where realism sees power as the primary currency of international politics, idealism sees institutions, norms, and the internal character of states. Where realism treats the anarchic quality of the international system as a fixed constraint that policy must work within, idealism sees it as a condition that can be ameliorated through the construction of international institutions, the spread of democratic governance, and the development of shared norms that constrain state behavior.

The most influential articulation of idealist foreign policy in American history was Woodrow Wilson's vision for the post-World War I international order. Wilson argued that the war had been caused not by the normal operation of the balance of power system — states competing for security in an anarchic environment — but by the specific pathologies of authoritarian governments, which pursued aggressive foreign policies to serve the interests of ruling elites rather than the interests of their populations. The solution was not to restore the pre-war balance of power but to transform the international system — through the spread of democratic self-governance, the establishment of international institutions capable of resolving disputes peacefully, and the creation of norms of collective security that would make aggression unprofitable.

Word help: liberal internationalism = the idea that democracy and cooperation among countries keep the peace · norms = shared rules of behavior · pathologies = unhealthy habits · authoritarian = ruled by one person or a small group with no real elections · League of Nations = Wilson's proposed world organization · collective security = countries agreeing to defend each other · Fourteen Points = Wilson's 1918 plan for peace

Chapter 18, Section I, “Idealism: The Logic of Values and Democratic Peace.”

Source AWilson's Fourteen Points: A League of Nations

President Woodrow Wilson laid out the Fourteen Points to Congress on January 8, 1918, as a plan for peace after World War I. Point XIV proposed the idea that became the League of Nations. Primary source.

“A general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for the purpose of affording mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike.”

Word help: covenants = formal promises · mutual guarantees = promises each side makes to the other · territorial integrity = a country's borders staying safe · general association = a broad group

Woodrow Wilson, Address to Congress ("Fourteen Points"), January 8, 1918, Point XIV. The Avalon Project, Yale Law School, avalon.law.yale.edu/20th_century/wilson14.asp.

Idealism in Wilson's words. Use Source A and Reading E. What does Wilson want countries to do, and how does that fit idealism rather than realism?

Reading FAfter the League: Postwar Institutions and Democratic Peace

Wilson's vision was defeated at home by the Senate's rejection of the League of Nations and abroad by the failure of the peace settlement to create the conditions for genuine democratic self-determination in Europe and Asia. But the idealist tradition he represented did not disappear; it was revived and institutionalized in the post-World War II order that the United States played the leading role in constructing. The United Nations, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, and the network of human rights treaties and institutions that developed in the postwar decades all reflect the idealist premise that durable peace and prosperity require not just a favorable balance of power but a set of international institutions and norms capable of managing the relationships among nations in ways that reduce the risk of conflict and promote cooperative problem-solving.

The democratic peace theory — the empirical observation that liberal democracies have rarely, if ever, gone to war with each other — provides perhaps the strongest analytical foundation for idealist foreign policy. If democracies do not fight each other, then the spread of democratic governance is not merely a humanitarian aspiration but a strategic investment: a world of democracies is a world in which the risk of great-power conflict is dramatically reduced. This argument has been used to justify American support for democratic transitions in various regions and has been a persistent element of American foreign policy thinking across administrations of both parties, though its application has been contested and its results uneven.

Word help: self-determination = a people choosing its own government · United Nations, World Bank, IMF, GATT = postwar organizations for peace and trade · human rights treaties = agreements protecting basic rights · democratic peace theory = the observation that democracies rarely fight each other · empirical = based on evidence · ameliorated = made better

Chapter 18, Section I, “Idealism: The Logic of Values and Democratic Peace.”

Reading GThe Hybrid Reality

In practice, American foreign policy has never been purely realist or purely idealist. Most successful American foreign policy has been a pragmatic hybrid — drawing on realist analysis to assess the distribution of power and identify vital interests, while drawing on idealist principles to define the values that American power should serve and the international framework it should seek to construct. The architects of the postwar international order — Franklin Roosevelt, Harry Truman, George Marshall, and Dean Acheson — were realists in their recognition that American power would be the foundation of any stable postwar order, but idealists in their belief that durable stability required institutions, rules, and the spread of democratic governance rather than pure power politics.

The result was a foreign policy tradition that combined hard-headed assessment of national interests with genuine commitment to international institutions and human rights — a tradition sometimes called "liberal internationalism" or "American internationalism" that has been the default framework for American foreign policy since World War II, though it has been contested and strained by both isolationist impulses from the right and humanitarian interventionism from the left.

Word help: pragmatic = practical · hybrid = a mix of two things · hard-headed = realistic and unsentimental · internationalism = working with other countries · isolationist impulses = the urge to stay out · interventionism = stepping into other countries' conflicts

Part 3 of 9

The Invitation to Struggle

CORE OBJECTIVE

FQ 3: Analyze the constitutional "invitation to struggle" between the executive and legislative branches regarding war powers and treaties, explaining how the ambiguous distribution of foreign policy authority in the Constitution has produced recurring institutional conflict.

IN MY WORDS: Who is really in charge of foreign policy: the president or Congress?

Reading HDivided on Purpose

The Constitution's allocation of foreign policy authority between the president and Congress is one of the most deliberately ambiguous features of the founding document — and one of the most consequential sources of institutional conflict in American political history. The Framers divided foreign policy powers between the branches not out of oversight or confusion but out of a deliberate design philosophy: they were committed to preventing the concentration of power in any single institution, and they recognized that foreign policy presented particular risks of executive overreach given the traditional identification of kings with their nations' external relations.

Word help: allocation = how something is shared out · deliberately ambiguous = unclear on purpose · concentration = putting power in one place · executive overreach = the president taking too much power · Framers = the writers of the Constitution

Chapter 18, Section II, “The Institutional Struggle for Control.”

Why divide the power? Use Reading H. Why did the Framers split foreign policy powers between the branches instead of giving them all to the president?

Reading IThe President's Powers

The Constitution gives the president an impressive array of foreign policy powers. As commander-in-chief of the armed forces, the president has operational control over the military — the authority to direct the deployment, movement, and use of America's fighting forces in ways that no other institution can readily countermand. As the nation's chief diplomat, the president has the power to receive foreign ambassadors and ministers — a provision that implies the broader authority to recognize foreign governments and to conduct diplomatic relations — and to negotiate treaties with foreign nations. The president also has extensive appointment powers over the foreign policy apparatus: the Secretaries of State and Defense, the national security advisor, the director of national intelligence, and the ambassadors who represent the United States abroad are all presidential appointees.

Word help: commander-in-chief = the leader of the armed forces · chief diplomat = the top official in dealing with other countries · ambassadors = a country's official representatives abroad · recognize = officially accept a foreign government · national security advisor = the president's adviser on security · director of national intelligence = the head of the spy agencies

Reading JWhy Presidents Lead

The practical advantages of presidential leadership in foreign policy are substantial. In a world where threats can materialize rapidly and where the capacity to respond quickly and with secrecy can be strategically decisive, the presidency's institutional characteristics — unity of command, speed of decision, control of information, and continuity of engagement — provide capabilities that the deliberative, multi-member, publicly transparent legislative process cannot match. A president who decides that a specific foreign threat requires immediate action can order a military response within hours; a Congress that might want to authorize that same response would require weeks of committee hearings, floor debate, and vote scheduling even in the most cooperative political environment.

These advantages have led presidents throughout American history to assert broad executive authority over foreign policy — often pushing the boundaries of their constitutional authority in ways that they justify on grounds of strategic necessity. The practice of executive agreements — direct deals between the president and foreign heads of state or governments that have the practical force of treaties but do not require Senate ratification — has become one of the most important mechanisms through which presidents manage foreign relationships outside the formal treaty process. While the Constitution specifies that treaties require the advice and consent of two-thirds of the Senate, executive agreements have been used to establish significant international commitments without Senate approval — from the Destroyers for Bases agreement of 1940, through which Roosevelt provided Britain with fifty destroyers in exchange for naval base rights, to the Paris Agreement on climate change, which the Obama administration joined as an executive agreement rather than a treaty.

Word help: unity of command = one person in charge · secrecy = keeping information private · hearings = meetings where lawmakers question people · executive agreement = a deal made by the president that does not need Senate approval · Destroyers for Bases = a 1940 deal giving Britain 50 ships · Paris Agreement = a climate deal among countries · treaty = a formal agreement approved by the Senate

Chapter 18, Section II, “The President: Commander-in-Chief and Chief Diplomat.”

Reading KCongress: Purse and War Power

Despite the president's practical advantages in foreign policy, Congress retains significant constitutional authority over the nation's international affairs. The Constitution reserves to Congress the power to declare war — the most consequential of all foreign policy decisions. It gives Congress the power of the purse over all government spending, including the military appropriations that fund the armed forces and the foreign aid that supports American diplomatic relationships. It requires Senate ratification of treaties by a two-thirds majority — a provision that has given the Senate decisive leverage over major international agreements throughout American history. And it authorizes Congress to establish the military through legislation, to regulate commerce with foreign nations, and to define the conditions under which the president may use military force.

Word help: power of the purse = Congress's control over spending · appropriations = money Congress sets aside · ratification = official approval · regulate commerce = make rules for trade · leverage = influence

Part 4 of 9

War Powers in Practice

CORE OBJECTIVE

FQ 3: Analyze the constitutional "invitation to struggle" between the executive and legislative branches regarding war powers and treaties, explaining how the ambiguous distribution of foreign policy authority in the Constitution has produced recurring institutional conflict.

IN MY WORDS: Why hasn't Congress declared war since 1942, even though the U.S. has fought several wars?

Reading LNo Declaration Since 1942

The constitutional declaration of war power has been a persistent source of institutional tension. Congress has formally declared war only eleven times in American history — the last time in 1942, following the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor. Every significant military engagement since then — Korea, Vietnam, the Gulf War, Afghanistan, Iraq — has been conducted under other legal authorities: United Nations resolutions, congressional authorizations that fall short of formal declarations, or the president's claimed inherent authority as commander-in-chief. This pattern has fundamentally altered the constitutional balance of war power, concentrating effective decision-making authority in the executive branch while leaving Congress in the position of either acquiescing after the fact to military commitments the president has already made, or risking the political costs of appearing to abandon American forces already in harm's way.

Word help: formally declared = officially announced by a vote of Congress · authorizations = permissions · inherent authority = power that comes with the office · acquiescing = going along without objecting · concentrating = gathering in one place

Chapter 18, Section II, “Congress: The Power of the Purse and the Constitutional War Power.”

Reading MThe War Powers Resolution

The Vietnam War — which by the late 1960s had produced more than fifty thousand American deaths, massive domestic political upheaval, and a profound crisis of public confidence in government — produced the most significant congressional attempt to reclaim the war power: the War Powers Resolution of 1973. Passed over President Nixon's veto, the Resolution requires the president to notify Congress within forty-eight hours of deploying troops into hostilities, and mandates their withdrawal within sixty days — extendable by thirty days for safety reasons — unless Congress specifically authorizes the mission. The Resolution was an attempt to restore congressional oversight over the decision to commit the nation to armed conflict without preventing the president from responding rapidly to genuine emergencies.

Word help: War Powers Resolution (1973) = a law meant to limit presidents' use of troops without Congress · hostilities = fighting · veto = the president's rejection of a bill · notify = officially tell · public confidence = people's trust · oversight = supervision

Source CThe War Powers Resolution (1973)

Congress passed this resolution over President Nixon's veto on November 7, 1973, near the end of the Vietnam War. Section 2(c) says when the president may use the armed forces in fighting. Primary source.

“The constitutional powers of the President as Commander-in-Chief to introduce United States Armed Forces into hostilities, or into situations where imminent involvement in hostilities is clearly indicated by the circumstances, are exercised only pursuant to (1) a declaration of war, (2) specific statutory authorization, or (3) a national emergency created by attack upon the United States, its territories or possessions, or its armed forces.”

Word help: imminent = about to happen · pursuant to = following · statutory authorization = permission written into a law · national emergency = a sudden crisis threatening the country

Joint Resolution Concerning the War Powers of Congress and the President (War Powers Resolution), November 7, 1973, Section 2(c). The Avalon Project, Yale Law School, avalon.law.yale.edu/20th_century/warpower.asp.

Reading NA Law That Has Not Held

In practice, however, the War Powers Resolution has not meaningfully constrained presidential military action. Presidents since its passage have consistently denied its constitutional validity — arguing that it impermissibly limits the president's constitutional authority as commander-in-chief — while simultaneously complying with its notification requirements as a matter of courtesy rather than legal obligation. Congress, faced with the political difficulty of withdrawing support from troops already deployed, has rarely exercised the resolution's withdrawal mechanism. The result has been a chronic condition of unconstitutional presidential military action and congressional acquiescence — a pattern that has allowed the executive branch to conduct extended military operations in Korea, Vietnam, Lebanon, Grenada, Libya, Somalia, Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, and numerous other locations without the formal declaration of war that the Constitution requires.

Word help: constitutional validity = whether a law fits the Constitution · courtesy = politeness, not a duty · withdrawal mechanism = the rule forcing troops to come home · acquiescence = going along · chronic = lasting a long time

Chapter 18, Section II, “Congress: The Power of the Purse and the Constitutional War Power.”

Part 5 of 9

Isolationism and Its End

CORE OBJECTIVE

FQ 4: Trace the evolution of American strategy from isolationism through the World Wars, the Cold War's doctrine of containment, and the complex interdependencies of the modern globalized order, explaining what forces drove each major strategic transition.

IN MY WORDS: Why did the United States avoid alliances for 150 years, and what finally changed that?

Reading OWashington's Advice

The founders who crafted American foreign policy in the republic's early decades were guided by a clear-eyed assessment of the nation's strategic position: a relatively weak, commercially oriented republic situated at a considerable distance from the great powers of Europe, with no military capable of competing on the European continent and no interest in the dynastic quarrels and imperial competitions that consumed European political energy. George Washington's Farewell Address of 1796 — one of the most influential documents in the history of American foreign policy — warned against "permanent alliances" with any portion of the foreign world, arguing that entanglement in European conflicts would compromise American independence and drain resources that could better be spent on domestic development.

Word help: permanent alliances = long-lasting military partnerships · entanglement = being drawn into someone else's conflict · commercially oriented = focused on trade · dynastic quarrels = fights among royal families · imperial competitions = struggles over colonies · compromise = weaken

Chapter 18, Section III, “From the Founding to Pearl Harbor: The Long Era of Isolationism.”

Visual DWashington's Farewell Address (1796)

Use this printing of the Farewell Address with Reading O.

What to look for: The page is mostly printed text, with a title across the top. Ask: Why would an outgoing president address "the people" instead of Congress? The portrait is a small engraving.

Chapter image reproduced from the chapter PDF; credited in the chapter caption as a public-domain / government item (origin not independently re-verified).

Reading PA Century of Restraint

This counsel of strategic restraint was well-suited to the republic's first century. Protected by the Atlantic Ocean, benefiting from the relative decline of European interest in North American affairs, and focused primarily on continental expansion and economic development, the United States could afford to treat European politics largely as spectators rather than participants. The Monroe Doctrine of 1823, which warned European powers against further colonization of the Western Hemisphere, staked out a regional sphere of American influence while reaffirming the principle of non-entanglement in European affairs. The Civil War and its aftermath consumed domestic political energy for decades, reinforcing the inward orientation of American strategic thinking.

And even as American economic and industrial power grew to rival and ultimately surpass the great powers of Europe in the late nineteenth century, the political culture and strategic habits of isolationism remained dominant, sustained by geographic advantage, commercial success, and a deep cultural suspicion of the militarism and power politics associated with European statecraft.

Word help: strategic restraint = holding back on purpose · Monroe Doctrine (1823) = a warning to Europe not to colonize the Americas · hemisphere = half of the world · continental expansion = growing across North America · militarism = putting military power first · spectators = watchers, not players

Chapter 18, Section III, “From the Founding to Pearl Harbor: The Long Era of Isolationism.”

The Monroe Doctrine. Use Reading P. What did the Monroe Doctrine of 1823 warn against, and how did it fit the idea of non-entanglement in Europe?

Reading QEmpire, War, and the Return of Isolationism

The Spanish-American War of 1898 and its aftermath — which produced American control over the Philippines, Puerto Rico, and Guam — briefly challenged the isolationist consensus by raising the possibility of American empire in Asia and the Caribbean. But the anti-imperialist reaction that followed, combined with the reluctance of subsequent administrations to sustain the commitments that empire required, limited the transformation. When World War I erupted in Europe in 1914, President Woodrow Wilson's initial response was neutrality — a position that reflected the overwhelming preference of the American public to remain outside a European conflict that seemed distant and incomprehensible.

American entry in 1917, justified by Germany's unrestricted submarine warfare and the interception of the Zimmermann Telegram (in which Germany proposed a military alliance with Mexico against the United States), was experienced by much of the public as a departure from rather than an expression of American strategic interest. The Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Versailles and the League of Nations in 1919 and 1920 represented the political reassertion of the isolationist tradition — the refusal of the most powerful deliberative body in American government to accept the permanent international commitments that Wilson's idealist vision required.

The United States retreated into the interwar period with its isolationist habits largely intact, even as fascism rose in Europe and militarism expanded in Asia. It took the shock of Pearl Harbor to demonstrate, with a finality that no argument had previously achieved, that the geographic insulation that had sustained American isolationism was no longer adequate protection in an era of modern warfare.

Word help: anti-imperialist = against building an empire · neutrality = not taking sides · unrestricted submarine warfare = sinking ships without warning · Zimmermann Telegram = a German message proposing an alliance with Mexico against the U.S. · Treaty of Versailles = the 1919 peace treaty after World War I · interwar = between the wars · fascism = a harsh, one-party dictatorship

Part 6 of 9

The Cold War and Containment

CORE OBJECTIVE

FQ 4: Trace the evolution of American strategy from isolationism through the World Wars, the Cold War's doctrine of containment, and the complex interdependencies of the modern globalized order, explaining what forces drove each major strategic transition.

IN MY WORDS: How did the United States try to stop the spread of Soviet power without fighting World War III?

Reading RA New Kind of Rival

The strategic transformation produced by World War II was immediate, comprehensive, and durable. The United States emerged from the war as the world's dominant military and economic power — the only major combatant whose industrial capacity had expanded rather than been destroyed, the possessor of the world's only nuclear arsenal, and the principal architect of the postwar international institutional order. But the rapid deterioration of relations with the Soviet Union, the communist takeover of Eastern Europe, the Soviet development of nuclear weapons in 1949, and the outbreak of the Korean War in 1950 confronted American policymakers with a strategic challenge unlike any they had previously faced: a global ideological and geopolitical competition with an adversary of comparable military capability whose expansionist ambitions threatened to upset the postwar balance of power.

Word help: dominant power = the strongest country · industrial capacity = ability to make goods · nuclear arsenal = nuclear weapons · communist = tied to a one-party system that controls the economy · expansionist = wanting to take more land and influence · ideological = based on a set of beliefs

Chapter 18, Section III, “The Cold War and the Architecture of Containment.”

Why was the USSR different? Use Reading R. Name two facts that made the Soviet Union a different kind of challenge than any the U.S. had faced before.

Visual EMissile Launch Site in Cuba (1 November 1962)

Reading SContainment

The strategic framework that emerged from this challenge — containment — was most systematically articulated by diplomat and scholar George Kennan in his famous 1946 "Long Telegram" and his 1947 "X Article" in the journal Foreign Affairs. Kennan argued that the Soviet Union, while ideologically committed to the expansion of communist power, was not willing to risk direct military confrontation with the United States. The appropriate American response was therefore not to attempt to roll back Soviet power through military action, but to contain it — to maintain sufficient countervailing force at the strategic points where Soviet expansion was most likely, to support the economic recovery and political stability of countries vulnerable to communist subversion, and to wait with patience for internal contradictions within the Soviet system to produce its eventual transformation or collapse.

Word help: containment = the strategy of stopping the spread of Soviet power without all-out war · George Kennan = the diplomat who explained containment · Long Telegram = Kennan's 1946 message · X Article = Kennan's 1947 magazine article · roll back = push back by force · countervailing force = an opposing force · subversion = secret efforts to weaken a government

Chapter 18, Section III, “The Cold War and the Architecture of Containment.”

Reading TTruman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, NATO

Containment found its institutional expression in a series of landmark policy commitments. The Truman Doctrine, announced before Congress in March 1947, committed the United States to providing political, military, and economic support to "free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures" — a formulation broad enough to justify American support for governments threatened by communist movements anywhere in the world. The Marshall Plan, proposed by Secretary of State George Marshall in June 1947 and ultimately providing approximately $13 billion in economic assistance to Western European nations recovering from the war, rested on the premise that economic desperation was the primary recruiter for communist parties in war-devastated societies, and that robust economic recovery was therefore a strategic investment in containing Soviet influence.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organization, established in 1949, created a formal multilateral military alliance among the United States, Canada, and Western European nations — the first permanent peacetime military alliance in American history and a direct expression of the commitment to collective defense against Soviet aggression.

Word help: Truman Doctrine = the 1947 promise to help free peoples resisting takeover · Marshall Plan = U.S. aid to rebuild Western Europe · NATO = the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a defense alliance · multilateral = involving several countries · multilateralism = working with other countries together · unilateralism = acting alone · subjugation = being forced under someone's control · collective defense = members protecting each other

Part 7 of 9

After the Cold War: Interdependence

CORE OBJECTIVES

FQ 4: Trace the evolution of American strategy from isolationism through the World Wars, the Cold War's doctrine of containment, and the complex interdependencies of the modern globalized order, explaining what forces drove each major strategic transition.

FQ 1: Essential Question: How does the United States strategically balance the pursuit of national interests with the promotion of global democratic values?

IN MY WORDS: What replaced containment as the main idea in American foreign policy?

Reading UNo Single Plan

The end of the Cold War in 1991 — announced by the dissolution of the Soviet Union on Christmas Day of that year — confronted American foreign policy with a strategic vacuum. The containment framework that had organized American strategy for four decades had been rendered obsolete by the disappearance of the adversary it was designed to contain. The decade that followed was characterized by a series of ad hoc responses to regional crises — humanitarian intervention in Somalia and Bosnia, NATO expansion into the former Soviet bloc, the development of free trade agreements including NAFTA and the creation of the World Trade Organization — without a coherent strategic framework comparable to containment to organize them.

The September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks provided a new organizing principle — the "Global War on Terror" — but this framework proved inadequate to the complexity of the strategic environment, leading to the extended and costly military engagements in Afghanistan and Iraq that dominated American strategic attention for the first two decades of the twenty-first century. The gradual rise of China as a peer competitor — not just economically but technologically and eventually militarily — has since emerged as the dominant strategic challenge facing American foreign policy, one that requires a fundamentally different strategic response than either Cold War containment or post-9/11 counterterrorism.

Word help: dissolution = breaking up · strategic vacuum = a gap with no guiding strategy · humanitarian intervention = sending help or troops to stop suffering · NAFTA = the North American Free Trade Agreement · World Trade Organization (WTO) = the group that sets trade rules · Global War on Terror = the name for the post-2001 effort against terrorist groups · peer competitor = a rival of about equal strength

Chapter 18, Section III, “Modern Interdependency and the Challenges of a Multipolar World.”

Visual FEras of American Strategy

What to look for: Read left to right. Notice that the third box has no single guiding idea. Ask: What changed between boxes one and two?

Original diagram made for this assignment from Chapter 18, "The Evolution of American Strategy." Dates are approximate.

Reading VInterdependency

The concept of interdependency captures a central feature of the contemporary international environment that distinguishes it from the Cold War era. Nations today are linked by trade, finance, technology, information, and migration in ways that create both unprecedented opportunities for prosperity and unprecedented vulnerabilities to disruption. The United States depends on global supply chains for critical goods including pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, and rare earth minerals. American financial markets are deeply integrated with those of Europe, Asia, and the emerging economies of the developing world. American companies compete globally, depend on international markets for their growth, and employ workers and operate facilities across dozens of countries.

This interdependency creates powerful incentives for peaceful cooperation — conflict among deeply interdependent economies is enormously costly for all parties — but it also creates vulnerabilities that adversaries can exploit through economic coercion, supply chain manipulation, and targeted financial sanctions.

Word help: interdependency = countries relying on each other for trade, money, technology, and people · supply chains = the networks that make and move goods · semiconductors = computer chips · rare earth minerals = metals used in electronics · coercion = forcing someone to act · sanctions = penalties on a country · vulnerabilities = weak points

Part 8 of 9

Tools of Foreign Policy

CORE OBJECTIVE

FQ 5: Evaluate the tools of foreign policy — including economic sanctions, foreign aid, military force, diplomacy, and soft power — and assess the conditions under which each is most effective in advancing American objectives.

IN MY WORDS: Which tools "push" other countries and which "pull" them?

Reading WHard Power: Force

Hard power — the use of military force or economic pressure to compel changes in other nations' behavior — represents the most direct and most costly dimension of the American foreign policy toolkit. Military force is the ultimate guarantor of American security and the foundation of American credibility in the international system: the knowledge that the United States possesses the world's most capable military and has demonstrated the willingness to use it shapes the calculations of both adversaries and allies in ways that diplomatic words alone cannot achieve. American military power serves several distinct strategic functions: deterrence, persuading potential adversaries that the costs of aggression will outweigh any possible gains; compellence, using the threat or application of force to change behavior that has already occurred; defense, protecting American territory and citizens from attack; and power projection, extending American influence and protecting American interests in regions distant from the American homeland.

Word help: hard power = using force or economic pressure to make others act · deterrence = discouraging attack by showing the cost · compellence = using threats to change behavior · power projection = reaching far from home with military strength · credibility = being believed

Chapter 18, Section IV, “Hard Power: Force and Economic Coercion.”

Reading XSanctions and Foreign Aid

Economic sanctions represent a form of hard power that operates between the extremes of diplomacy and military force — coercive measures designed to impose economic costs on a target government in the hope of compelling a change in behavior without the direct human costs of armed conflict. The United States has imposed sanctions on dozens of countries over the course of the past century, targeting behaviors ranging from nuclear weapons development to human rights violations to support for terrorism. Sanctions instruments include trade embargoes that prohibit the import or export of specified goods, asset freezes that block access to funds held in the United States, and secondary sanctions that impose costs on third-country entities that do business with the sanctioned nation.

The effectiveness of sanctions as a foreign policy instrument is contested: they impose genuine costs on target economies and can contribute to diplomatic pressure, but they are often unable by themselves to produce changes in core strategic behavior, particularly among authoritarian governments that are willing to impose economic pain on their own populations to resist external pressure. Foreign aid — the provision of economic, humanitarian, military, or technical assistance to other nations — serves a different strategic function, one that lies closer to the boundary between hard and soft power. Military aid, provided to allied and partner governments to strengthen their capacity to defend themselves and conduct operations alongside American forces, is clearly an instrument of hard power strategy.

Economic and humanitarian aid serves a different set of objectives: building the economic stability and political legitimacy of partner governments, creating conditions in which extremist movements find less fertile ground for recruitment, and generating the goodwill and access that enable American diplomacy to be effective. Critics argue that foreign aid is a costly and ineffective use of taxpayer resources; defenders respond that the entire foreign aid budget — approximately one percent of total federal spending — represents a small investment in the prevention of the far larger costs of instability, conflict, and humanitarian crisis.

Word help: economic sanctions = penalties on a country's trade or money · embargo = a ban on trade · asset freeze = blocking a government's money · secondary sanctions = penalties on others who trade with the target · foreign aid = money or help sent to other countries · extremist = holding very harsh and violent views · authoritarian = ruled by one person or small group

Reading YSoft Power

The concept of soft power — developed most systematically by political scientist Joseph Nye — captures a dimension of international influence that operates through attraction and persuasion rather than through coercion and payment. Hard power compels; soft power attracts. A nation with significant soft power can shape the preferences of other nations and their populations — making them more likely to support American objectives, more willing to accept American leadership, and more inclined to adopt American values and institutional models — without having to resort to threats or incentives. The sources of American soft power are considerable: the attractiveness of American culture and entertainment, the reputation of American universities and scientific institutions, the appeal of American political values and democratic ideals, and the perception that American leadership of the international system has produced broadly shared benefits rather than serving only American interests.

Word help: soft power = influence through attraction and persuasion · Joseph Nye = the political scientist who developed the idea · persuasion = convincing · preferences = what people want · institutional models = ways of organizing government · reputation = how others see you

Reading ZDiplomacy

Diplomacy — the direct management of relationships among nations through negotiation, communication, and the building of shared frameworks for cooperation — is the primary instrument through which soft power is exercised. The State Department and its network of embassies, consulates, and diplomatic missions across the world conduct the continuous work of American diplomacy: negotiating international agreements, managing bilateral relationships with specific countries, representing American interests in multilateral forums like the United Nations, and providing the day-to-day communication through which misunderstandings are prevented and conflicts are managed before they escalate. Public diplomacy — efforts to communicate directly with foreign publics rather than just foreign governments, through cultural exchange programs, educational initiatives, and media outreach — extends the reach of American diplomatic influence beyond the formal channels of government-to-government communication.

Word help: diplomacy = managing relations between countries through talks · State Department = the agency that runs U.S. diplomacy · embassies = offices of a country in another country · multilateral forums = meetings of many countries, like the UN · bilateral = between two countries · public diplomacy = reaching ordinary people abroad

Part 9 of 9

New Threats and the Big Question

CORE OBJECTIVES

FQ 6: Assess the impact of modern global challenges — including terrorism, cyber warfare, and climate change — on traditional concepts of national security, explaining why these non-state and transnational threats require fundamentally different strategic responses than the state-based threats of earlier eras.

FQ 1: Essential Question: How does the United States strategically balance the pursuit of national interests with the promotion of global democratic values?

IN MY WORDS: Why do threats from groups and computer networks need different answers than threats from other countries?

Reading AAThreats Without a Return Address

The security challenges that dominated American foreign policy in the early decades of the twenty-first century — and that will continue to shape it for the foreseeable future — differ fundamentally from the state-based threats that organized American strategy during the Cold War. The Soviet Union, for all its danger, was a conventional adversary: a recognized state with identifiable leadership, a defined territory, an economy, and a population that created both vulnerabilities and accountabilities. The threat it posed could be addressed through conventional instruments of statecraft — alliances, deterrence, arms control negotiations, and economic competition.

The threats posed by non-state terrorist organizations, hostile cyber operations, and global climate change share a common characteristic: they cannot be addressed through these conventional instruments alone, because they do not originate from the kind of actors that conventional diplomacy and military strategy are designed to manage.

Word help: non-state actors = groups that are not governments · conventional = traditional · accountabilities = ways to hold someone responsible · transnational = crossing borders · deterrence = discouraging attack by threatening punishment · adversary = enemy

Chapter 18, Section IV, “New Frontiers: Terrorism, Cyber Warfare, and the Redefinition of Security.”

Visual KAn Airman Monitors Networks

Use this photograph with Reading AB and Reading AC.

What to look for: The monitors show network activity. Ask: Where is the "battlefield" in cyber defense? Notice there are no weapons visible, only computers.

Chapter image reproduced from the chapter PDF; credited in the chapter caption as a public-domain / government item (origin not independently re-verified).

Reading ABTerrorism and Its Limits

The September 11, 2001 attacks demonstrated the catastrophic potential of non-state terrorist organizations operating without territory, without conventional military capability, and without the accountability structures that make deterrence effective against state actors. A government that fears retaliation can be deterred; a terrorist organization willing to sacrifice its members in service of a cause cannot be deterred in the same way. The American response — the invasion of Afghanistan to destroy al-Qaeda's sanctuary and training infrastructure, followed by the invasion of Iraq based on disputed intelligence about weapons of mass destruction — demonstrated both the extraordinary military capability of American conventional forces and the severe limitations of conventional military power in addressing decentralized, ideologically motivated non-state threats that can regenerate their capacity faster than conventional military operations can destroy it.

Word help: al-Qaeda = the terrorist group that carried out the 2001 attacks · sanctuary = a safe place · weapons of mass destruction = weapons that can kill huge numbers of people · decentralized = not run from one central place · regenerate = grow back

Chapter 18, Section IV, “New Frontiers: Terrorism, Cyber Warfare, and the Redefinition of Security.”

Write the letter of the best answer, then explain in one sentence how the reading shows it.

Reading ACCyber Warfare

Cyber warfare represents an even more challenging frontier for traditional security concepts. Foreign governments, criminal organizations, and non-state actors have demonstrated the capacity to penetrate American government and private sector computer networks, to steal sensitive information, to manipulate critical infrastructure, and to conduct influence operations targeting American democratic processes. These capabilities are difficult to attribute — sophisticated cyber operations can be designed to obscure their origins — and even more difficult to deter through conventional means, since the threat of military retaliation against a cyber attack requires both reliable attribution and a willingness to escalate to conventional conflict that may be disproportionate to the harm inflicted.

The protection of American digital infrastructure — the power grid, the financial system, transportation networks, and military command and control systems — has become one of the most urgent and most complex challenges in American national security.

Word help: cyber warfare = attacks carried out through computer networks · penetrate = break into · critical infrastructure = systems a country needs to run, like power and banks · influence operations = efforts to shape what people believe · attribution = proving who did it · escalate = make a conflict bigger · disproportionate = too big for the harm done

Why deterrence fails. Use Reading AB. Explain why deterrence works against a government but is harder against a terrorist organization.

Reading ADA Crowded World

The strategic landscape that American foreign policy must navigate in the third decade of the twenty-first century is more complex, more dangerous, and in some respects less favorable to American interests than at any point since the early Cold War. China's rise as a peer competitor — combining economic scale, technological sophistication, military modernization, and a strategic ambition to reshape the international order in ways that serve Chinese interests — poses the most significant long-term challenge to American primacy. Russia's continued willingness to use military force to revise the European security order, demonstrated most clearly in its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, has revived the prospect of great-power conflict in Europe that the Cold War's end seemed to have permanently retired.

The proliferation of nuclear weapons technology to unstable or hostile states, the accelerating impacts of climate change, and the capacity of social media and information operations to manipulate democratic publics all add dimensions to the security environment that no previous generation of American strategists has had to manage simultaneously.

Word help: multipolar = having several major powers · primacy = being first · peer competitor = a rival of about equal power · revise = change · proliferation = spread of weapons · information operations = efforts to shape people's beliefs online · landscape = overall situation

Chapter 18, Section IV, “The Responsibility of Power in a Multipolar World.”

Three challenges. Use Reading AD. Name three of the challenges that the chapter says American strategists must now manage at the same time.

Reading AEConclusion: Interest and Values

The essential question this chapter poses — how the United States strategically balances the pursuit of national interests with the promotion of global democratic values — does not admit of a permanent answer. The balance has shifted repeatedly as the international environment has changed, as American power has grown and, in some respects, been tested, and as the lessons of strategic experience have been absorbed and applied. The isolationism of the founding era gave way to reluctant internationalism after Pearl Harbor; Cold War containment gave way to the complex, less clearly organized strategic landscape of the post-Cold War and post-9/11 eras; and the emerging multipolar order of the twenty-first century is demanding yet another strategic adaptation.

This is not just a strategic question; it is a democratic one. In a republic, the decisions that commit the nation's resources and risk its citizens' lives in service of foreign policy objectives must ultimately be made with the consent of the governed — through the constitutional mechanisms of congressional authorization, public deliberation, and electoral accountability. The challenge of conducting a coherent, strategically effective foreign policy within those democratic constraints is the enduring and unresolved tension at the heart of American engagement with the world.

Word help: essential question = the big question of the chapter · adaptation = change to fit new conditions · finite = limited · congressional authorization = Congress giving its approval · electoral accountability = voters being able to remove leaders · consent of the governed = the people's approval · enduring = lasting

Chapter 18, Conclusion.

Source FWashington's Farewell Address (1796)

President George Washington published this address on September 19, 1796, as he left office. It is often cited as the root of the American tradition of avoiding entanglement in foreign affairs. Primary source.

“The great rule of conduct for us in regard to foreign nations is in extending our commercial relations, to have with them as little political connection as possible. . . . It is our true policy to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world; so far, I mean, as we are now at liberty to do it; for let me not be understood as capable of patronizing infidelity to existing engagements.”

Word help: commercial relations = trade · political connection = formal ties in government and defense · permanent alliances = lasting military partnerships · existing engagements = agreements already made · patronizing infidelity = supporting breaking a promise
